data_section_full_text:
4. Data description


The identity of auditors in all publicly listed Swedish companies is obtained from Finansinspektionen (The Swedish Financial Supervisory Authority). The initial sample is restricted
to those engagement partners that audited at least one publicly listed company during
2003–2007. I have manually collected information on audit fees and nonaudit fees for the
period 2003–2007 from the annual reports of Swedish listed companies. Data on the home
offices of audit partners were obtained from the records of Revisorsnamnden (The Supervisory Board of Public Accountants), which is a governmental authority under the Ministry of Justice. The Board handles matters relating to chartered accountants and chartered
accounting firms.

Data on individual audit partners’ personal client portfolios and financial statement
information from sample companies is retrieved from Upplysningscentralen AB (UC AB),
which is Sweden’s largest business and credit information agency and is owned by the
major Swedish banks. UC AB’s database contains information on all enterprises registered
in Sweden. Because UC AB does not report data on audit fees, I measure (within-industry)
client portfolio size using either the aggregate amount of audited total assets or the aggregate number of engagements. Industry classifications are based on the Swedish Standard
Industrial Classification Codes (SNI2002), which in turn are based on the European standards for industry classifications (NACE). <sup>17</sup> It is important to note that while the client
portfolio measures include both public and private Swedish companies, the final empirical
analyses are restricted to the publicly listed companies.

To rule out confounding auditor-type effects I exclude clients of non–Big 4 accounting
firms. I also exclude all joint audits since they further complicate the issue of who determines audit fees. In a joint audit, the audit report is signed by two auditors from different
audit firms that are jointly liable for the issued opinion. Financial sector and firm-years
with incomplete data for the empirical models have been excluded. The final sample consists of 862 firm-year observations from 206 unique nonfinancial firms for which there are
total of 171 individual audit partners.
